name: Eudeve
confidence_why: Eudeve is extinct and every reading rests on the acute accents of one 17th-century missionary grammar: Manaster Ramer (1996) takes them as a lexically contrastive accent inherited from Proto-Uto-Aztecan while granting they may mark tone rather than stress, Lionnet (1985) reads them as a basic root-initial accent displaced only under suffixation and compounding, and Shaul (1983) says stress usually falls on the second syllable or a suffix but may be initial.

catalog_quote: However, Eudeve and Huichol preserve clear evidence of this reconstructed PUA accentual contrast. In Eudeve, we cannot be sure what exactly was meant by the acute accent mark in the grammar and vocabulary now published by Pennington (1981). The anonymous 17th century Spanish author who wrote it could have been hearing stress or tone, but at least it seems likely that it was a prosodic feature of some kind. ... Crucially in both languages, in certain morphological classes, the acute accent appears to fall with almost perfect consistency on the syllable which I reconstruct as stressed in PUA. ... In Eudeve, we find the contrast only in one set of verb forms. Noun stems of both *CVCV and *CVCVC classes show accent on the second syllable in the nominative case and on the first syllable (the second syncopates) in the accusative and genitive, e.g., surá-t, súr-ta, súr-te 'seed' < PUA *sula ju…

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Eudeve has an empty rule, so this adds content rather than agreeing or contradicting; internally it hedges between second-syllable/suffix stress and initial stress. It partly conflicts with Lionnet 1985 (index 2), who places the basic accent on the first syllable of the root.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Comparative note, not a rule: Eudeve (with Opata and Tubar) 'usually' stresses the second syllable or a suffix, but Opata and Eudeve 'may have initial stress', and in the same section 'development of initial stress' is listed as an innovation shared by Opata-Eudeve and Cahitan. The cited forms in the paper's word list are marked with an acute accent for stress (fn. 2) and show both initial (e.g. Eu sīwa-t 'belly', héwa 'bone', mári 'daughter') and second-syllable (e.g. Eu hakí-t 'arroyo', napósa- 'ashes') stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress 'may have been variable with respect to verb morphology' in Uto-Aztecan (citing Heath 1977); Table 2 (p. 104) is meant to show the patterns but the scanned of it is unreadable.
new_statements.identity_note: Lionnet 1985 distinguishes two Eudeve varieties: En = northern Eudeve (anonymous 'Arte y vocabulario de la lengua eudeve, heve o dohema', speech of Batuc / the Cucurpe-San Miguel river area) and Es = southern Eudeve (Loaysa's 'Arte de la lengua hegue', Onavas); his root-initial accent claim is stated for 'Eudeve, or at least En'. Shaul 1983 uses Eudeve data from Lionnet (1979a) and Escalante (1964) without specifying a variety. Shaul 1991 (not opened) is a morphosyntax overview of the same extinct language from the colonial sources.

new_statements.quote: En los demás grupos el acento tiene, en los morfemas raíces que son generalmente disílabos, una posición básica: de ésta se desplaza solamente en ciertos compuestos, siempre de una sílaba a la que sigue. [...] c. En los demás grupos, parece que la posición básica del acento coincide con la primera sílaba de la raíz. [...] Pensamos haber demostrado en un estudio anterior (LIONNET, sin fecha) que no era otro e1 caso del eudeve o por lo menos de En. Por eso damos, en e1 anexo, los radicales del idioma en su forma básica por ejemplo, a1 leer en e1 manuscrito anónimo: atét (caso sujeto), átta (caso objeto), "piojo", transcribimos simplemente: áte-, "piojo".
new_statements.translation: In the other groups [i.e. all Sonoran groups except Tubar] the accent has, in root morphemes, which are generally disyllabic, a basic position: from this it moves only in certain compounds, always by one syllable to the following one. [...] c. In the other groups [Tepiman, Opata-Eudeve, Cahita], it seems that the basic position of the accent coincides with the first syllable of the root. [...] We believe we showed in an earlier study (LIONNET, undated) that the case of Eudeve, or at least of En [northern Eudeve], was no different. That is why we give, in the annex, the language's radicals in their basic form; for example, on reading in the anonymous manuscript atét (subject case), átta (object case), 'louse', we simply transcribe áte-, 'louse'. (The 'e1'/'a1' in the quote are typesetting artifacts for 'el'/'al' in the re-typeset PDF.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The basic accent falls on the first syllable of the (usually disyllabic) root; it shifts rightward by one syllable only in certain compounds. The introduction's summary table gives 'Sílaba tónica: Primera' for Opata-Eudeve (OE), against second syllable for Tarahumara-Guarijío and final for Tubar. The example atét (subject) / átta (object) 'louse' shows surface accent moving with the case suffix, which Lionnet abstracts to the root form áte-.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shifts one syllable to the right in certain compounds; the claim is made explicitly for Eudeve 'or at least En' (the northern variety of the anonymous Arte y vocabulario), citing an undated earlier study by Lionnet; the source forms are 17th-18th-century missionary manuscripts, so the statement is philological.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Spot-checks of the not-opened work: bibliographic record; its datapoints are all syntax/morphology, none stress) and the DOI (recheck 403, an automated-access block). Nothing about stress found in either, and no genuine open copy of Shaul 1991 exists at the listed or derived URLs. Nothing missed in the two on-disk works beyond the two additions noted in the evidence: Table 2 of Shaul 1983 (p. 104) is legible from the page scan and marks Eudeve stress as optional/variable in four of six correspondence sets; Lionnet 1985's annex contains roughly 45 second-syllable-accented Eudeve radicals against roughly 115 initial ones.

readall_conflicts: The one listed work (Shaul 1991) could not be opened, so nothing new from it. Between the two works already held by the project there is a partial disagreement: Shaul 1983 (KWPL, p. 100) says that in Opata, Eudeve and Tubar stress 'usually' falls on the second syllable or a suffix, then adds that Opata and Eudeve 'may have initial stress' and lists 'development of initial stress' as an innovation shared by Opata-Eudeve and Cahitan; Lionnet 1985 (Amerindia 10, sec. 1) states that in Opata-Eudeve the basic accent sits on the first syllable of the root (shifting one syllable right only in certain compounds), with surface alternations such as atét / átta 'louse' abstracted to root-initial áte-. The surface second-syllable stresses Shaul cites (hakí-t, napósa-) are what Lionnet treats as suffix-induced shifts from a root-initial base, so the sources differ on analysis and on how regular the initial pattern is, not on the raw data.

tone.quote: NOTA 53 Cuando. Este se puede explicar con héco (cuando) de modo que se ponga acento en la primera (sílaba), pues poniéndolo en la última es ¿cuándo?, interrogativo. [...] Pararse muchos así se dice vóisindo hábeme con el acento en la primera [sílaba] porque habéme con el acento en la segunda [sílaba] es venirse muchos. [...] óvi. A estas horas. El acento en la primera [sílaba]. oví. Carbón. Brasa.
tone.locator: Arte, 'Notas', Nota 53; Vocabulario s.v. merisíndo húehren (p. 203) and s.v. óvi / oví (p. 215); further pairs s.v. chutzán/chútzan (p. 176), hecó/héco (p. 185), héqui (p. 186), híbe (p. 187); editor's introduction on accent inconsistencies pp. 25-26
tone.translation: NOTE 53. 'When'. This can be expressed with héco (when) provided the accent is put on the first (syllable), for putting it on the last makes it 'when?', interrogative. [...] For many to stop (standing) one says vóisindo hábeme with the accent on the first [syllable], because habéme with the accent on the second [syllable] is 'for many to come'. [...] óvi. At this hour. The accent on the first [syllable]. oví. Charcoal. Ember.
tone.summary: No tone statement; the 17th-c. Arte records a contrastive accent position (lexical and grammatical minimal pairs héco/hecó, hábeme/habéme, óvi/oví, chútzan/chutzán) without saying whether 'acento' is stress or pitch; the compilers notes the manuscript's accent marks are inconsistent.
